---
title: Installing Software
---

![*Sandwich*, [xkcd #149](https://xkcd.com/149/) by Randall Munroe, used under [CC BY-NC 2.5](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc/2.5/)](/images/xkcd-149-sandwich.png){fig-alt="Two stick figures. The first says: make me a sandwich. The second: what? make it yourself. The first says: sudo make me a sandwich. The second: okay."}

That joke is the whole of this chapter. There are things the computer will not
do when you ask, and does when you ask with `sudo` in front.

Along the way we will install some software we do not have yet, which is a
skill in itself. In this chapter, we'll learn about the following commands:

* `whoami` - print who you are
* `which` - show where a command lives
* `sudo` - run one command as the administrator
* `apt` - install and remove software
* `figlet`, `cowsay` - two silly programs to install

The silly ones are not filler. In the next chapter we will need commands that
produce plenty of text on demand, and these two are exactly that.

## A command we do not have

Let's try a command you almost certainly do not have yet.

```session
$ figlet hello
Command 'figlet' not found, but can be installed with:
sudo snap install figlet  # version 2.2.5+git24.202a0a8, or
sudo apt  install figlet  # version 2.2.5-3
sudo apt  install toilet  # version 0.3-1.4
See 'snap info figlet' for additional versions.
```

Compare that with the error from the first chapter, when we typed `dat` by
mistake:

```session
$ dat
bash: dat: command not found
```

Both commands are missing, but the computer treats them differently. `dat` is
nobody's command, so there is nothing to say about it. `figlet` is a real
program that simply is not on this machine - and Ubuntu knows that, because it
keeps a list of every program it could give you. So instead of stopping at
"not found", it tells you how to get it.

That is what the rest of this chapter is about. Ignore the `snap` line, and the
suggestion of `toilet`. We will use the second one:

```
sudo apt install figlet
```

Two commands we have never seen, so let's take them one at a time - `sudo`
first.

## Who are you?

The `whoami` command prints your username.

```session
$ whoami
anand
```

No surprise there. But watch what happens when we put `sudo` in front of it:

```session
$ sudo whoami
root
```

The same command, run by somebody else.

**root** is the administrator account on a Unix machine - the one that is
allowed to change anything, anywhere. `sudo` means "run this one command as
root". Just this one; when it finishes, you are yourself again.

## Why `sudo` is needed at all

Try the install without it:

```session
$ apt install figlet
E: Could not open lock file /var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend - open (13: Permission denied)
E: Unable to acquire the dpkg frontend lock (/var/lib/dpkg/lock-frontend), are you root?
```

Permission denied - and the message ends by asking the relevant question, *are
you root?*

Here is the reason. Everything we have made so far lived in your home
directory, which belongs to you. Installing a program is different: it puts a
file into `/usr/bin`, a directory shared by everyone who uses the machine. One
person's mistake there is everybody's mistake, so the system does not let an
ordinary user write to it.

That is not an obstacle to work around. It is the reason you can experiment in
your own directory without any fear of breaking the computer.

## Your password, and the silence

The first time you run a `sudo` command in a session, it asks for your
password:

```session
$ sudo apt update
[sudo] password for anand:
```

Type your own login password and press Enter.

::: {.callout-warning}
Nothing appears as you type - no letters, no dots, no stars. The cursor does
not move. This is deliberate, so that nobody reading over your shoulder can
count the characters. Type the password and press Enter even though the screen
looks like it is ignoring you.
:::

After that, `sudo` stops asking for a few minutes, so a run of `sudo` commands
does not mean a run of passwords.

## Refreshing the list

Ubuntu keeps a catalogue of the software available to you: names, versions and
where to download each one. `sudo apt update` fetches a fresh copy of that
catalogue.

```session
$ sudo apt update
Hit:1 http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu resolute InRelease
Hit:2 http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu resolute-updates InRelease
Hit:3 http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu resolute-security InRelease
Reading package lists... Done
Building dependency tree... Done
Reading state information... Done
205 packages can be upgraded. Run 'apt list --upgradable' to see them.
```

Yours will differ - a different number of packages, and `Get:` instead of
`Hit:` on lines where there was something new to fetch. What matters is that
it ends without an error.

Run this before installing anything, especially on a machine you have just set
up. Without it, `apt` is working from whatever catalogue it last downloaded,
which may be months old and may point at versions that are no longer there.

::: {.callout-warning}
`update` and `upgrade` sound alike and do different things. `sudo apt update`
refreshes the *list*. `sudo apt upgrade` installs newer versions of everything
you already have, which can take a long time. We only need `update` here.
:::

## Installing a package

Software on Ubuntu comes in **packages**. A package is one program - or one
library, or one set of data files - wrapped up with its name, its version, and
a note of whatever else it needs in order to work. `apt` is the command that
installs them.

```session
$ sudo apt install figlet
Reading package lists... Done
Building dependency tree... Done
Reading state information... Done
The following NEW packages will be installed:
  figlet
0 upgraded, 1 newly installed, 0 to remove and 205 not upgraded.
Need to get 133 kB of archives.
After this operation, 752 kB of additional disk space will be used.
Get:1 http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu resolute/universe amd64 figlet amd64 2.2.5-3 [133 kB]
Fetched 133 kB in 1s (125 kB/s)
Selecting previously unselected package figlet.
(Reading database ... 125595 files and directories currently installed.)
Preparing to unpack .../figlet_2.2.5-3_amd64.deb ...
Unpacking figlet (2.2.5-3) ...
Setting up figlet (2.2.5-3) ...
Processing triggers for man-db (2.10.2-1) ...
```

That is a lot of output for one small program, and you do not have to read all
of it. It says, in order: what will be installed, how much will be downloaded,
the download itself, and then the unpacking and setting up. The last lines
scroll past and the prompt comes back.

Did it work? `which` tells you where a command lives:

```session
$ which figlet
/usr/bin/figlet
```

There it is, in `/usr/bin` - the shared directory we were not allowed to write
to a moment ago. `sudo` is what let `apt` put it there.

## Having some fun

`figlet` prints text in large letters made of ordinary characters.

```session
$ figlet hello
 _          _ _
| |__   ___| | | ___
| '_ \ / _ \ | |/ _ \
| | | |  __/ | | (_) |
|_| |_|\___|_|_|\___/
```

It knows several styles, called fonts, and `-f` chooses one. It is an option,
like the `-i` we gave to `cp`:

```session
$ figlet -f digital hello
+-+-+-+-+-+
|h|e|l|l|o|
+-+-+-+-+-+
```

```session
$ figlet -f small Craft of Computing
  ___           __ _          __    ___                     _   _
 / __|_ _ __ _ / _| |_   ___ / _|  / __|___ _ __  _ __ _  _| |_(_)_ _  __ _
| (__| '_/ _` |  _|  _| / _ \  _| | (__/ _ \ '  \| '_ \ || |  _| | ' \/ _` |
 \___|_| \__,_|_|  \__| \___/_|    \___\___/_|_|_| .__/\_,_|\__|_|_||_\__, |
                                                 |_|                  |___/
```

Which fonts are there? A package installs more than the program itself, and
`figlet`'s fonts are plain files sitting in `/usr/share/figlet`. We know how to
look at a directory that is not our own, and we know how to ask for just the
files we want:

```session
$ ls /usr/share/figlet/*.flf
/usr/share/figlet/banner.flf    /usr/share/figlet/script.flf
/usr/share/figlet/big.flf       /usr/share/figlet/shadow.flf
/usr/share/figlet/block.flf     /usr/share/figlet/slant.flf
/usr/share/figlet/bubble.flf    /usr/share/figlet/small.flf
/usr/share/figlet/digital.flf   /usr/share/figlet/smscript.flf
/usr/share/figlet/ivrit.flf     /usr/share/figlet/smshadow.flf
/usr/share/figlet/lean.flf      /usr/share/figlet/smslant.flf
/usr/share/figlet/mini.flf      /usr/share/figlet/standard.flf
/usr/share/figlet/mnemonic.flf  /usr/share/figlet/term.flf
```

An absolute path from chapter two, and a wildcard from chapter four, used to
poke around inside a package we installed a minute ago. Take the name of any of
those files without the `.flf` and hand it to `-f`.

## When apt asks a question

Installing `figlet` went straight through without asking us anything. That is
not always so, and the difference confuses people, so let's see the other case.

The message at the start of the chapter also suggested `toilet`, which does the
same job as `figlet` with fancier characters. Install that one and watch what
happens:

```session
$ sudo apt install toilet
Reading package lists... Done
Building dependency tree... Done
Reading state information... Done
The following additional packages will be installed:
  libcaca0 toilet-fonts
The following NEW packages will be installed:
  libcaca0 toilet toilet-fonts
0 upgraded, 3 newly installed, 0 to remove and 205 not upgraded.
Need to get 950 kB of archives.
After this operation, 1929 kB of additional disk space will be used.
Do you want to continue? [Y/n]
```

And there it stops. Nothing else happens, no new prompt appears, and it can
look as though the terminal has frozen. It has not. `apt` has asked a question
and is waiting for you to answer it.

Look at why it asked. We named one package and the list says **three** will be
installed. `toilet` cannot work on its own: it needs `libcaca0` and
`toilet-fonts`. Packages a package needs are called its **dependencies**, and
`apt` works them out for you - but since it is about to do more than you asked
for, it shows you the list first.

To answer, type `y` and press Enter, or `n` and press Enter to change your
mind. The capital letter in `[Y/n]` is the default, so pressing Enter on its
own also means yes. Let's do that:

```session
Do you want to continue? [Y/n]
Get:1 http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu resolute-updates/main amd64 libcaca0 amd64 0.99.beta19-2.2ubuntu4.2 [224 kB]
Get:2 http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu resolute/universe amd64 toilet-fonts all 0.3-1.4 [714 kB]
Get:3 http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu resolute/universe amd64 toilet amd64 0.3-1.4 [12.7 kB]
Fetched 950 kB in 2s (526 kB/s)
Unpacking libcaca0:amd64 (0.99.beta19-2.2ubuntu4.2) ...
Unpacking toilet-fonts (0.3-1.4) ...
Unpacking toilet (0.3-1.4) ...
Setting up toilet (0.3-1.4) ...
Processing triggers for man-db (2.10.2-1) ...
```

Three packages downloaded and set up, because we asked for one.

```session
$ toilet -f smblock craft
         ▗▀▖▐
▞▀▖▙▀▖▝▀▖▐  ▜▀
▌ ▖▌  ▞▀▌▜▀ ▐ ▖
▝▀ ▘  ▝▀▘▐   ▀
```

::: {.callout-tip}
If an `apt` command seems to be taking forever, look at the last line on the
screen. Nine times out of ten it is a `[Y/n]` question waiting for an answer.
:::

## A second package, and a wrinkle

```session
$ sudo apt install cowsay
Reading package lists... Done
Building dependency tree... Done
Reading state information... Done
Suggested packages:
  filters cowsay-off
The following NEW packages will be installed:
  cowsay
0 upgraded, 1 newly installed, 0 to remove and 205 not upgraded.
Need to get 18.6 kB of archives.
After this operation, 93.2 kB of additional disk space will be used.
Get:1 http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu resolute/universe amd64 cowsay all 3.03+dfsg2-8 [18.6 kB]
Fetched 18.6 kB in 1s (26.4 kB/s)
Selecting previously unselected package cowsay.
(Reading database ... 125611 files and directories currently installed.)
Preparing to unpack .../cowsay_3.03+dfsg2-8_all.deb ...
Unpacking cowsay (3.03+dfsg2-8) ...
Setting up cowsay (3.03+dfsg2-8) ...
Processing triggers for man-db (2.10.2-1) ...
```

```session
$ cowsay hello
 _______
< hello >
 -------
        \   ^__^
         \  (oo)\_______
            (__)\       )\/\
                ||----w |
                ||     ||
```

Now the wrinkle. Ask where it went:

```session
$ which cowsay
/usr/games/cowsay
```

Not `/usr/bin` this time, but `/usr/games`. Ubuntu keeps the frivolous programs
apart from the serious ones, and both directories are places the shell looks
when you type a command name. There is nothing to fix here - it is worth seeing
only because it makes the point that a command is just a file sitting somewhere,
and `which` will tell you where.

`cowsay` has other animals, kept as files in the same way `figlet` keeps fonts:

```session
$ ls /usr/share/cowsay/cows
apt.cow                fox.cow           sheep.cow
bud-frogs.cow          ghostbusters.cow  skeleton.cow
bunny.cow              gnu.cow           snowman.cow
calvin.cow             hellokitty.cow    stegosaurus.cow
cheese.cow             kangaroo.cow      stimpy.cow
cock.cow               kiss.cow          suse.cow
cower.cow              koala.cow         three-eyes.cow
daemon.cow             kosh.cow          turkey.cow
default.cow            luke-koala.cow    turtle.cow
dragon-and-cow.cow     mech-and-cow.cow  tux.cow
dragon.cow             milk.cow          unipony-smaller.cow
duck.cow               moofasa.cow       unipony.cow
elephant-in-snake.cow  moose.cow         vader-koala.cow
elephant.cow           pony-smaller.cow  vader.cow
eyes.cow               pony.cow          www.cow
flaming-sheep.cow      ren.cow
```

`-f` picks one, exactly as it did for `figlet`:

```session
$ cowsay -f tux The command line is fun
 _________________________
< The command line is fun >
 -------------------------
   \
    \
        .--.
       |o_o |
       |:_/ |
      //   \ \
     (|     | )
    /'\_   _/`\
    \___)=(___/
```

## Installing several at once

`apt install` takes as many package names as you like, in the same way `touch`
and `rm` do. We could have installed both of ours in one command:

```session
$ sudo apt install figlet cowsay
Reading package lists... Done
Building dependency tree... Done
Reading state information... Done
cowsay is already the newest version (3.03+dfsg2-8).
figlet is already the newest version (2.2.5-3).
0 upgraded, 0 newly installed, 0 to remove and 205 not upgraded.
```

We already have them, so `apt` did nothing and said so - no question asked,
nothing downloaded.

That is worth knowing in general: installing something you already have is
harmless. When instructions tell you to run an `apt install`, you can run it
without first working out whether you need to.

## Reading about a package

If you want to know what a package is before installing it, `apt show` prints
its description. This one needs no `sudo`, because it only reads:

```session
$ apt show figlet
Package: figlet
Version: 2.2.5-3
Priority: optional
Section: universe/text
Origin: Ubuntu
Installed-Size: 752 kB
Depends: libc6 (>= 2.14)
Homepage: http://www.figlet.org/
Download-Size: 133 kB
APT-Sources: http://archive.ubuntu.com/ubuntu resolute/universe amd64 Packages
Description: Make large character ASCII banners out of ordinary text
 FIGlet (Frank, Ian & Glenn's Letters) is a program that creates large
 characters out of ordinary screen characters.
```

Notice `Depends: libc6`. Most packages need other packages, and `apt` works
that out and installs them too - that is the "and 3 newly installed" you
sometimes see when you asked for one thing.

## Removing a package

`sudo apt remove` takes a package away again. We have had our fun with
`toilet` and do not need it, so:

```session
$ sudo apt remove toilet
Reading package lists... Done
Building dependency tree... Done
Reading state information... Done
The following packages will be REMOVED:
  toilet
0 upgraded, 0 newly installed, 1 to remove and 205 not upgraded.
After this operation, 49.2 kB disk space will be freed.
Do you want to continue? [Y/n] y
Removing toilet (0.3-1.4) ...
Processing triggers for man-db (2.10.2-1) ...
```

The same question as before, and here the list above it is the part to read.
`apt` will happily take other packages along with the one you named, and this
is where it tells you. Answer `n` if the list is not what you expected.

Keep `figlet` and `cowsay` - the next chapter uses them.

## Being careful with sudo

`sudo` lifts the one restriction that has been protecting you all along. The
system stops you from damaging the machine; `sudo` says "yes, I mean it".

So, two habits:

* Use `sudo` when a command genuinely needs it - installing software, mostly.
  It is not a magic word to add when something does not work.
* Never paste a `sudo` command you found on the internet without reading it
  first. `sudo` will run it, and it will not ask whether you understood it.

The commands in this chapter are the ordinary use of `sudo`, and there is
nothing to be nervous about. Just notice each time you type it.

::: {.callout-tip}
## On a Mac

macOS has no `apt`. The usual equivalent is [Homebrew](https://brew.sh/),
which you install once by following the instructions on its website. After
that, `brew install figlet cowsay` does the job of this chapter's `apt`
commands, and `brew` needs no `sudo`, because it installs into a directory
that belongs to you.

These notes assume Ubuntu, on a Linux machine or through WSL on Windows.
:::

## Summary

| Command | What it does |
|---------|--------------|
| `whoami` | prints your username |
| `sudo whoami` | prints `root` - the command ran as the administrator |
| `which figlet` | shows where a command lives |
| `sudo apt update` | refreshes the list of available packages |
| `sudo apt install figlet` | installs a package |
| `sudo apt install figlet cowsay` | installs more than one |
| `apt show figlet` | describes a package, without installing it |
| `sudo apt remove toilet` | removes a package |
| `figlet hello` | prints `hello` in large letters |
| `figlet -f small hello` | uses a different font |
| `cowsay hello` | a cow says `hello` |
| `cowsay -f tux hello` | a different animal says it |

And the question `apt` asks: `Do you want to continue? [Y/n]` is waiting for
`y` or `n` and Enter. Enter on its own means yes.

And the one idea to carry forward: your own files are yours to break, and the
rest of the machine is not - which is why installing software needs `sudo`, and
why nothing else you have done so far has.
